entries.old: rare
entries.new: limited
entries.note: Canada says credit cards are 'not widely accepted' and the UK says some ATMs and many banks take foreign cards; 'rare' overstated it.

entries.old: Spring (April–May) and fall (September–October) …
entries.new: No official seasonal guidance; Canada's rainy season March–May
entries.note: Model-written seasonal advice replaced; Canada's travel advice gives only the rainy season.

entries.new: withdrawn

entries.new: UK, Canada and Australia advise against all travel

entries.old: … Solo women travelers report being refused hotels and services …
entries.new: UK and Canada rules, attributed

entries.new: deleted

entries.new: Canada and UK statements, with the cash limits
entries.note: Money-market claim removed; answer rewritten from Canada's and the UK's money sections.

entries.old: general 112
entries.new: general 112, ambulance 127, fire 128
entries.note: FCDO lists ambulance 127, fire 128 and 112 (as police and for emergency services); the separate police line 129 that only Canada lists is not shown.
Seasonal recommendation withdrawn: no official source names a best time to visit; text now states the FCDO weather hazards.

entries.old: Flying a drone requires prior authorization from the Albanian civil aviation authority — do not fly without a permit.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source we could read supports this; withdrawn.

entries.old: Summer lines at the land borders with Montenegro and North Macedonia can run to hours around weekends — cross early in the morning if you can.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source we could read supports this; withdrawn.

entries.new: (removed)

entries.old: police: 17 · ambulance: 14
entries.new: police: 17 · ambulance: 1021 · fire: 14
entries.note: Ambulance is 1021 per UK FCDO "Getting help"; 14 is the fire service.

entries.old: The Algerian dinar is not convertible abroad — change money inside Algeria, keep exchange receipts and spend or re-exchange dinars before departure.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says you must declare all foreign currency on arrival and report each exchange during your stay, and show the declaration form and bank exchange receipts when you leave. Algerian dinars cannot be taken out of the country.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice states.

entries.old: Drones may not be brought in without prior authorization and are routinely confiscated at the border.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says it is illegal to bring drones, binoculars, telescopes and certain types of photography equipment into Algeria without authorisation; check with Algerian customs before you travel.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice states.

entries.old: Plan around cash: exchange euros or dollars at banks or hotels, keep the receipts, and re-exchange leftover dinars before you leave. The dinar cannot be changed abroad.
entries.new: Plan around cash: Canada's travel advice says cards are rarely accepted outside major hotels. Change money only at banks or official exchange bureaus, keep the receipts — you must show them when you leave — and do not take dinars out of the country.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice states.

entries.old: Avoid areas close to the borders with Libya, Mali, Mauritania and Niger — governments warn of terrorism and kidnapping risk there, and travel in much of the deep Sahara requires escorts arranged through your agency.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller advises against all travel within 450 km of the borders with Mali and Niger and within 100 km of the borders with Mauritania, Libya and Tunisia because of terrorism and kidnapping. It also says that, by law, police must approve road travel outside city limits in advance.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice states; the escort claim is not in any official source.

entries.old: Do not photograph government buildings, police, military sites or infrastructure. It can lead to questioning or detention.
entries.new: Do not photograph military sites, government buildings, bridges or security personnel — Canada says photographing sensitive installations is prohibited, and Australia says it is illegal.
entries.note: Consequence claim removed; rewritten to official travel advice.

entries.old: Rarely — only some upscale hotels and a few ATMs accept international cards. Bring cash in euros or dollars, exchange as needed, and keep receipts so you can re-exchange dinars before leaving, as the dinar is not convertible abroad.
entries.new: Rarely. Canada's travel advice says credit cards are usually accepted at major hotels but rarely in restaurants and other businesses, and that ATMs taking foreign cards are unreliable. It also says you must keep bank receipts for every exchange and that dinars cannot be taken out of the country.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice states.

entries.new: Canada's travel advice says it is illegal to take turtle shells or ivory out of Angola, and that customs may keep handicrafts considered to be of cultural value.

entries.old: Photography of government buildings, ports, airports and military sites is prohibited.
entries.new: Canada advises against photographing airports, major roads, bridges, communications installations, military personnel and government buildings, and the UK warns not to use cameras, binoculars or GPS equipment near government buildings.

entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the currency is the East Caribbean dollar (XCD) and that US dollars are widely accepted. No official source we could read describes card acceptance.
entries.note: Rewritten to what Canada's advice states; the card-acceptance claim and the EC$2.60/2.70 exchange rates had no official source.

entries.old: December to April is dry, breezy and reliably sunny. May to November is hotter and wetter, with the hurricane peak from August to October, but far cheaper.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit. Canada's travel advice says the hurricane season runs from early June to the end of November.

entries.old: Foreign cards are now widely accepted and charged at a market exchange rate, so paying by card is usually the simplest option; the old "blue dollar" cash premium has largely disappeared since the exchange-rate unification, though US dollar notes remain useful as backup. Inflation means peso prices change quickly.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says foreign credit and debit cards are accepted in main cities, and that you may be asked for photo ID, such as a copy of your passport, when paying by card. ATM withdrawals from foreign bank accounts are subject to low per-withdrawal and daily limits, and substantial service charges may apply.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the cited official source says.

entries.old: October to April (the southern spring, summer and fall) suits most itineraries — essential for Patagonia, pleasant in Buenos Aires and the wine regions; June–August is ski season in the Andes.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives seasonal travel guidance for Argentina.
entries.note: Withdrawn: no official seasonal guidance found.

entries.old: Personal electronics such as a laptop and phone enter duty-free; keep receipts for expensive new items.
entries.new: (removed or rewritten)
entries.note: Not stated by an official source we could read; removed or replaced with what the source says.

entries.old: Strict controls apply to fresh food, plants and animal products, especially when crossing into Patagonia.
entries.new: (removed or rewritten)
entries.note: Not stated by an official source we could read; removed or replaced with what the source says.

entries.old: Pay by foreign card where possible — international cards are settled at a market exchange rate since the FX unification, so the old need to carry stacks of US dollars for the "blue" rate has mostly gone. Keep some USD notes as backup and expect peso prices to move with inflation.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says ATM withdrawals on foreign bank cards are subject to low per-withdrawal and daily limits and can carry substantial service charges, so check with your bank before you travel.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Ferries from Buenos Aires reach Colonia del Sacramento and Montevideo in Uruguay in 1–2 hours. Bring your passport, as you clear both countries' immigration at the terminal (Mercosur nationals can use ID cards).
entries.new: (removed)

entries.old: Tap water is safe to drink in Buenos Aires and most Argentine cities; in remote rural areas ask locally or use bottled water.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: Withdrawn: no official source we could read supports it.

entries.old: Keep phones off café tables and be alert for distraction thefts ("mustard scam") in Buenos Aires tourist areas — petty theft, not violent crime, is the main visitor risk.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office reports distraction thefts in Buenos Aires such as the "mustard scam": thieves take your bags while an accomplice offers to clean off mustard they have sprayed on you. If it happens, politely but firmly refuse help and walk away.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Cards now work well: foreign Visa and Mastercard payments are converted at a market exchange rate, so card payments are usually as good as cash. Carry some US dollars or pesos as backup for small vendors and rural areas, and expect prices in pesos to rise frequently with inflation.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says foreign credit and debit cards are accepted in main cities, but ATM withdrawals on foreign cards are subject to low limits and substantial service charges may apply. You may be asked for photo ID, such as a copy of your passport, when paying by card.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources say, attributed.

entries.old: It is not an entry requirement for Argentina, but the Ministry of Health counts Misiones (where Iguazú is), Corrientes, Formosa and parts of Jujuy, Salta and Chaco as yellow fever risk areas and recommends vaccination at least 10 days before visiting areas with transmission. Brazil-side visits make it even more advisable.
entries.new: It is not an entry requirement for Argentina, but the Ministry of Health counts Misiones (where Iguazú is), Corrientes, Formosa and parts of Jujuy, Salta and Chaco as yellow fever risk areas and recommends vaccination at least 10 days before visiting areas with transmission.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources say, attributed.

entries.new: The Government of Canada notes that the import and export of cultural and historical items is regulated in Armenia, including archaeological objects, sculptures and paintings, ancient books and documents, musical instruments, furniture and carpets.

entries.old: Tap-to-pay by card or phone is the default everywhere, including buses and market stalls; many venues are effectively cashless. Tipping is not expected.
entries.new: No official source we could read describes how widely cards are accepted in Australia. Canada's travel advice notes only that the currency is the Australian dollar (AUD).
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Spring (September–November) and fall (March–May) suit most of the country; December–February is beach season in the south but wet season in the tropical north, where June–August is the prime dry season.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season runs from November to April, when severe flooding hits inland areas and cyclones can strike the coasts of Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia; bush fires are common between October and April.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Australia has some of the strictest biosecurity rules in the world: declare ALL food, plants, seeds, wooden items and animal products — undeclared items mean instant fines of hundreds of dollars and possible visa cancellation. | Duty-free allowance: 25 cigarettes and 2.25 liters of alcohol per adult. | Clean soil off shoes, camping and sports equipment before you fly — dirty gear can be seized for treatment.
entries.new: Declare all food, animal products and plant material (including wooden articles), and any footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals. Australia's Department of Agriculture says a false or misleading declaration can bring an infringement notice of up to AUD 7,280, civil penalty proceedings or prosecution, and visa cancellation. | Duty-free alcohol: 2.25 litres of alcoholic beverages per traveller aged 18 or over, according to the Australian Border Force. Most tobacco products are prohibited imports, though travellers aged 18 or over may bring tobacco products in without a permit. | The Department of Agriculture asks travellers to make sure footwear and sporting and recreational equipment are clean and free from soil, seeds and grass.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Declare every food item, plant product and wooden souvenir on your Incoming Passenger Card — even packaged snacks. Undeclared biosecurity items bring on-the-spot fines in the hundreds of dollars, and serious breaches can cancel your visa on the spot.
entries.new: Declare every food item, plant product and wooden souvenir on your Incoming Passenger Card. Australia's Department of Agriculture says declared goods are inspected and returned if they pose no biosecurity risk, while a false or misleading declaration can bring an infringement notice of up to AUD 7,280 and cancellation of your visa.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Australian UV levels are extreme even on cool or cloudy days. Use SPF 50+, a hat and sunglasses, and swim only between the red-and-yellow flags at patrolled beaches.
entries.new: Use SPF 50+, a hat and sunglasses, and swim only between the red-and-yellow flags at patrolled beaches.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Distances are vast: Sydney to Perth is further than London to Moscow. Fly between regions, plan fuel and water for outback drives, and avoid driving rural roads at dawn or dusk when kangaroos are active.
entries.new: Distances are vast. Fly between regions, plan fuel and water for outback drives, and avoid driving rural roads at dawn or dusk.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Only if you declare it. Australia's biosecurity rules are among the strictest in the world: all food, plant material and animal products must be declared on the Incoming Passenger Card. Many items are then allowed after inspection, but failing to declare brings immediate fines and can cancel your visa.
entries.new: Only if you declare it. All food, plant material and animal products must be declared on the Incoming Passenger Card. Australia's Department of Agriculture says declared goods are inspected and may be treated, exported or destroyed, and those that pose no biosecurity risk are returned; a false or misleading declaration can bring an infringement notice of up to AUD 7,280, civil penalties or prosecution, and visa cancellation.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Cards are widely accepted in cities and chains, but Austria keeps a strong cash culture. Many small restaurants, cafés, market stalls and mountain huts are cash-only.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says credit cards are widely accepted at main hotels, shops and restaurants, but smaller establishments may only accept cash. Australia's Smartraveller likewise says some businesses may only accept cash.
entries.note: Rewritten to what Canada's and Australia's travel advice say; the claims about mountain huts and market stalls had no source.

entries.old: May–September for cities, lakes and Alpine hiking; December for Christmas markets and the start of the ski season, which runs to March or April.
entries.new: No official source we checked gives seasonal guidance for Austria; the months shown are not an official recommendation. Australia's Smartraveller warns of avalanches, flash floods and mudslides in alpine areas, and says winter tyres are mandatory from 1 November to 15 April in winter conditions.
entries.note: The Christmas-market and ski-season claims had no official source; replaced with a neutral statement.

entries.old: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea). | No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
entries.new: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea). | Goods for your own use bought in another EU country carry no further duty. Above the EU guide levels (for example 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits), customs may ask you to show they are for personal use.
entries.note: EU rules: personal-use goods are not unlimited — customs may check quantities above the EU guide levels.

entries.old: Nearly all shops and supermarkets close on Sundays and public holidays — stock up on Saturday; only bakeries, station shops and restaurants stay open.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports the Sunday-closure claim.

entries.new: The UK FCDO says illegal drugs are strictly forbidden, even in residual amounts, and that you may need prior agreement from the authorities to bring prescription drugs into Bahrain — carry a doctor's note and check with a Bahraini embassy before you travel.

entries.new: During Ramadan the UK FCDO advises not eating, drinking, smoking or chewing gum in public in the daytime, including in your car. Hotels and restaurants that serve food in fasting hours may seat non-fasting guests separately.

entries.old: Cash rules. Cards are accepted only at larger hotels and supermarkets in Cotonou, while mobile money (MTN MoMo, Moov) is used everywhere. Reliable ATMs are mostly limited to Cotonou and larger towns.

entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: November to February is the main dry season — harmattan air, cooler nights and the best conditions for the coast, Ouidah and Abomey; the south sees heavy rain from April to July.

entries.old: Cards are accepted at better hotels and handicraft shops in Thimphu and Paro, but Bhutan is largely cash-based. The ngultrum is pegged 1:1 to the Indian rupee, and rupees are widely accepted.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says credit cards aren't widely accepted but can be used at major hotels, that EFTPOS is available nationwide including at most hotels, and that ATMs are common in towns. The Indian rupee is also legal tender, though larger notes may not be accepted.
entries.note: Rewritten to Australia's Smartraveller; the 1:1 peg and 'largely cash-based' claims had no source here.
September falls in the June–September monsoon named by Canada and Australia.

entries.old: Spring (March–May) brings rhododendron blooms and mild trekking weather; fall (September–November) offers the clearest Himalayan views and the biggest tsechu festivals.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the monsoon runs from June to September, when landslides are frequent and mountain roads can become impassable. No official source names a best season; the months shown fall outside the monsoon.
entries.note: Rhododendron and festival claims had no official source.

entries.old: Tobacco may be imported only in small quantities for personal use and attracts high duties; smoking is banned in most public places. | Antiques and religious artefacts may not be exported. Buy handicrafts from licensed shops and keep the receipts for customs.
entries.new: You can bring a small supply of tobacco for personal use, but the UK government says you must pay taxes and duties on it and be able to show proof of payment if asked; Canada's travel advice puts the tax at 200%. Smoking is prohibited in public places. | It is illegal to take antiques out of Bhutan, and customs officials may inspect items that look like antiques (UK government).
entries.note: Rewritten to the UK and Canadian advice; the religious-artefact and licensed-shop claims had no source.

entries.old: Only Drukair and Bhutan Airlines fly into Paro — one of the world's most demanding airports, where flights are weather-dependent and sell out around festival season. Book flights before anything else and keep a buffer day for connections.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports this tip.

entries.old: Since the 2023 reforms you can explore Thimphu and Paro independently, but a licensed guide is still required for treks and travel beyond the main western valleys. The rules are refined periodically, so check when applying. Most visitors simply book through a licensed Bhutanese operator.
entries.new: The UK government says you need to use tour guides when visiting places of interest, or you may be refused entry, and that permits are needed for some areas — your guide can arrange them.
entries.note: The 2023-reform claims about independent travel in Thimphu and Paro had no official source.

entries.old: Passes on popular routes climb well above 3,000 m and treks go much higher — build in acclimatisation days, and take even the day hike to Tiger's Nest (3,120 m) slowly.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says altitude sickness is a risk above 2,500 m, and Canada notes that several trekking trails exceed 5,000 m. Ascend slowly and make sure your insurance covers evacuation from altitude.
entries.note: Pass and Tiger's Nest heights had no official source.

entries.old: To enter dzongs and temples, wear long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt, remove shoes and hats, and photograph only where permitted — never inside shrine rooms.
entries.new: Dress respectfully when visiting temples and dzongs (UK government), and ask your guide before taking pictures or filming inside dzongs, temples and monasteries (Canada).
entries.note: Specific dress and photography rules had no official source.

entries.old: No — since the 2022–2023 reforms, independent visits are allowed and you can apply for the visa yourself. A licensed guide is still required for treks and for travel beyond the main western valleys, so many visitors find a licensed Bhutanese operator the simplest route.
entries.new: You can apply for the visa yourself at immi.gov.bt. But the UK government says you need to use tour guides when visiting places of interest, or you may be refused entry, and Canada's travel advice says you must buy a travel package from an authorised travel agent. Check with the Department of Immigration before planning an independent trip.
entries.note: The claim that independent visits need no guide contradicted UK and Canadian advice.

It also says Canadian dollars are hard to exchange, so bring US dollars if you need to exchange cash. The UK government says Bolivia is going through an economic crisis and a dollar shortage.

entries.old: Northern Botswana (Okavango, Chobe, Kasane) is a seasonal malaria area, especially November to April. Use repellent and consider prophylaxis; Gaborone and the south are essentially malaria-free.

entries.old: Expect veterinary checkpoints on main roads — raw meat and some animal products cannot be carried across foot-and-mouth control fences, and shoes and vehicle wheels may be disinfected.

entries.old: All travelers under 18 must carry a certified copy of their full (unabridged) birth certificate along with their passport. Minors traveling with one parent, or unaccompanied, should also carry consent letters from the absent parent(s). The rules mirror South Africa’s and are enforced.

entries.note: Canada: Bulgaria's economy is primarily cash-based.

entries.old: Bulgaria adopted the euro on January 1, 2026, replacing the lev. Cards are accepted widely in cities and resorts, but keep some cash for village restaurants, small guesthouses and rural areas, and expect some prices still displayed in both euro and old lev amounts.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Bulgaria's economy is primarily cash-based, though most businesses also accept major credit cards and ATMs are widely available. The UK Foreign Office says major credit and debit cards are accepted in most banks and hotels.
entries.note: Rewritten to what Canada and the FCDO state; the village/guesthouse and dual-pricing claims had no official source.

entries.old: May–September covers hiking in the Rila and Pirin mountains and the Black Sea beach season; December–March is ski season in Bansko and Borovets at some of Europe's lowest prices.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Bulgaria. The CIA World Factbook describes a temperate climate with cold, damp winters and hot, dry summers.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the hiking, beach and ski-season claims had no official source.

entries.old: ["Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air or sea).", "No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country."]
entries.new: ["Arriving from outside the EU, the EU's Your Europe portal gives a duty-free allowance of 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus 1 litre of spirits over 22% (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine); 200 cigarettes (or 250 g of tobacco) by air, but Bulgaria applies the lower limit of 40 cigarettes (or 50 g of tobacco) to travellers arriving by land or sea; and other goods worth up to €300, or €430 by air or sea. Under-17s get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.", "Between EU countries there is no fixed limit on goods for your own use, but Bulgaria may set guideline quantities for alcohol and tobacco, which cannot be lower than 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits.", "The UK Foreign Office says you cannot take meat, milk or products containing them into the EU, with some exceptions such as powdered baby milk and medically required foods."]
entries.note: Corrected: Bulgaria applies the lower 40-cigarette limit to land and sea arrivals; the wine and beer allowances were missing; 'no limits within the EU' replaced by the guideline-level rule.

entries.old: Bulgarian head gestures are famously reversed …
entries.new: (removed)

entries.new: FCDO taxi advice

entries.new: FCDO / Canada changeover statements

entries.old: Burkina Faso runs on cash and mobile money (Orange Money, Moov). Cards work only at a handful of hotels in Ouagadougou, and ATMs outside the two main cities are unreliable.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says most transactions in Burkina Faso are made in cash and recommends small bills, as change can be hard to get. ATMs are available in major cities; credit cards are accepted by some businesses in Ouagadougou, but their use is very limited outside the capital. Euros and US dollars are accepted in some establishments.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the cited official source says.

entries.old: November to February is the dry, relatively cool season — though any visit currently needs to be weighed against do-not-travel advisories; March to May is extremely hot.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season runs from June to October, when seasonal flooding can hamper overland travel and roads and bridges may become impassable.
entries.note: Rewritten to the climate statement the cited source makes.

entries.old: West African CFA franc (F CFA)
entries.new: CFA franc (FCFA)
entries.note: As the cited official source names it.

entries.old: The US, UK and most EU governments advise against all travel to Burkina Faso — if travel is unavoidable, arrange professional security support and keep plans flexible.
entries.new: The UK and Canadian governments both advise against all travel to Burkina Faso because of the threat of terrorism and kidnapping and the unstable political situation. If travel is unavoidable, arrange professional security support and keep plans flexible.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Overland routes and border areas are the most dangerous — attacks and IEDs occur on main roads, and several land borders are closed or restricted; fly in and out of Ouagadougou if you must go.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says terrorist attacks on major roads and transport routes are increasing, including with landmines and other explosive devices, particularly where terrorist groups operate and near border areas.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: The yellow fever certificate is checked on arrival. Carry the yellow card with your passport.
entries.new: A yellow fever certificate is required to enter Burkina Faso. Carry the yellow card with your passport.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Bring enough CFA franc cash or euros to exchange — card payments are rare even in Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says most transactions are made in cash and recommends small bills, as change can be hard to get; credit cards are accepted by some businesses in Ouagadougou, but their use is very limited outside the capital.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: For most travelers, no at present. The US, UK and most European governments advise against all travel due to terrorism and kidnapping risk across much of the country, including areas close to Ouagadougou. Check current advisories before making any plans.
entries.new: For most travelers, no at present. The UK and Canadian governments both advise against all travel to Burkina Faso because of the threat of terrorism and kidnapping and the unstable political situation. Check current advisories before making any plans.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources say, attributed.

entries.new: {"ambulance": "112", "police": "113"}
entries.note: Police 117 and fire 118 are not given by any official source read. The Government of Canada (newer) gives 112 for medical assistance and 113 for police; the UK FCDO gives 112 for ambulance, fire and police. No source gives a separate fire number.

entries.new: ["Kirundi", "French"]
entries.note: The Presidency lists Kirundi and French as the official languages; English (and Swahili) are described only as widely used, so English was removed from the official list.

entries.old: rare
entries.new: limited
entries.note: UK FCDO: cards rarely accepted outside Bujumbura; Government of Canada: large shops and hotels generally accept major cards. "Rare" overstated it.
The Presidency gives the dry season as June–August, not June–September.

entries.old: ["Plastic bags are banned in Burundi — repack your luggage into paper, cloth or reusable bags before arrival, as bags can be confiscated at the border."]
entries.note: No official source read states the plastic-bag ban or confiscation at the border; withdrawn.

entries.old: Portuguese, Cape Verdean Creole
entries.new: Portuguese, Cabo Verdean Creole (Crioulo)
entries.note: Named as the CIA World Factbook lists them (last archived copy).

entries.old: cards widely-in-cities, cash medium
entries.new: cards limited, cash medium
entries.note: Set to what the cited official source describes.

entries.old: Cards work in resort hotels, larger restaurants and supermarkets on Sal, Boa Vista and Santiago, but small guesthouses, taxis and markets want escudos. Euros are widely accepted in tourist areas. The escudo is pegged at about 110 to the euro.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says some hotels and restaurants accept major credit cards, and some hotels and restaurants in Praia convert US dollars and euros into local currency.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: November to April is dry and warm with steady trade winds — peak season for beaches, windsurfing and hiking on Santo Antão; August to October is more humid with occasional rain.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season runs from mid-August to mid-October and can bring flooding and landslides, and that sandstorms and dust storms are most likely in January and February.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Cape Verdean escudo
entries.new: Cabo Verde escudo
entries.note: Name as Canada's travel advice and ISO 4217 give it.

entries.old: Each island is distinct and connections take planning — internal flights and inter-island ferries sell out in season, and ferry schedules shift with the weather; book ahead.
entries.new: Each island is distinct and connections take planning: book internal flights and inter-island ferries ahead, and check ferry schedules close to departure.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Atlantic currents are strong and drownings happen every year off Santa Maria and Boa Vista — swim only at beaches locals recommend and heed flag warnings.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says strong currents and powerful waves make swimming dangerous in some places, and that several drownings occur every year, especially in Praia and on Sal. Swim only where locals recommend and heed flag warnings.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Euros are accepted almost everywhere tourists go, but change is given in escudos. Carry small notes and some CVE cash for markets and rural areas.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Yes, in most tourist areas — hotels, restaurants and excursion operators widely accept euros at the fixed rate of roughly 110 escudos per euro. You will still want escudos for markets, taxis and the quieter islands.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports it.

entries.old: Cambodia runs on cash, and US dollars circulate alongside the riel. Prices are often quoted in USD, with riel used for small change. Bring crisp, undamaged USD notes (torn bills are refused). Cards work only in upmarket hotels and restaurants.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says US dollars are widely used alongside the riel, but only newer, undamaged notes are accepted — notes with the slightest tear are refused. Credit cards are not widely accepted outside major cities, and ATMs are plentiful in Phnom Penh, Siem Reap and Sihanoukville but fewer in smaller towns.
entries.note: Rewritten to Canada's travel advice; the claims about prices quoted in USD and cards only in upmarket venues had no source.

entries.old: November to February is the cool, dry season — ideal for Angkor and the coast. March to May is very hot; June to October brings monsoon rains.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the dry season lasts from November to April and the rainy season from May to November; the UK government gives June to October for the monsoon. No official source names a best season.
entries.note: Replaced the Angkor/coast recommendation with the seasons the Canadian and UK advice give.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and up to 2 liters of alcohol per adult. | The customs declaration is part of the Cambodia e-Arrival form.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says the Cambodia e-Arrival forms cover immigration, customs and health, and must be completed within 7 days of your scheduled arrival.
entries.note: The duty-free allowance (200 cigarettes, 2 litres of alcohol) had no official source and was withdrawn.

entries.old: Apply for the eVisa only at the official evisa.gov.kh — lookalike sites charge inflated fees for the same 30 USD visa or sell fakes.
entries.new: Apply for the eVisa only on the official site, evisa.gov.kh.
entries.note: Claims about lookalike sites selling fakes had no official source.

entries.old: At land crossings (especially Poipet from Thailand), touts and even officials may demand extra "fees". The visa on arrival costs 30 USD flat. Pay in USD, refuse baht "conversions", and consider getting the eVisa beforehand.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports the overcharging claim; Australia's Smartraveller says land crossings with Thailand are currently closed.

entries.old: Carry small-denomination, crisp US dollar bills. Damaged or old-series notes are widely refused; change under 1 USD comes back in riel.
entries.new: Bring US dollar notes in good condition: Canada's travel advice says only newer, undamaged notes are accepted, and Australia's Smartraveller says sellers may refuse dirty, torn or high-value notes.
entries.note: The claim that change under 1 USD comes back in riel had no source.

entries.old: The Cambodia e-Arrival card is free — complete it at arrival.gov.kh or the official CeA app within 7 days before travel, and ignore paid third-party sites.
entries.new: The Cambodia e-Arrival card is free (UK government). If you arrive by air, complete it at arrival.gov.kh within 7 days before you arrive.
entries.note: The CeA app and third-party-site claims had no source.

entries.old: {"general": "117"}
entries.new: {"police": "117", "ambulance": "119", "fire": "118"}
entries.note: 117 is the police number, not a general one. Canada's advice (updated 14 August 2026) lists ambulance 119 and fire 118; the UK's (9 February 2026) lists ambulance 112 and fire 119 — the newer page was followed and the disagreement recorded.

entries.old: Cash is essential. Cards work only at major hotels and some supermarkets in Douala and Yaoundé. ATMs exist in cities but can be unreliable; mobile money (MTN MoMo, Orange Money) is used everywhere for day-to-day payments.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Cameroon is largely a cash-based economy and that credit cards are rarely accepted outside international hotels. The UK government says shops usually want small notes, which can be hard to get, that ATMs are not often available outside large towns, and that euros and US dollars are the most widely accepted foreign currencies.
entries.note: Mobile-money claims (MTN MoMo, Orange Money 'used everywhere') are unsourced and were removed.

entries.old: November to February — the main dry season — … heavy rains peak from July to October …
entries.new: No official seasonal guidance; Canada's rainy seasons by region
entries.note: Model-written seasons replaced with Canada's rainy-season dates, which differ from the old text.

entries.old: Drones may not be brought in or flown without prior authorization from the Cameroonian authorities.
entries.new: deleted
entries.note: No official source we could read says drones need prior authorisation to be brought in or flown.

entries.old: Export of ivory, protected wildlife products and unworked precious minerals is prohibited.
entries.new: UK: protected wildlife trade illegal without a licence
entries.note: The ivory and 'unworked precious minerals' export ban is unsourced; replaced with the UK's statement on protected wildlife.

entries.old: … most governments advise against all travel to these areas.
entries.new: UK, Canada and Australia advice, with the UK's exceptions
entries.note: 'Most governments' replaced with the governments whose advice we read.

entries.old: … mobile money is the easiest way to pay for taxis, markets and small hotels …
entries.new: UK statement on cash, ATMs and foreign currency
entries.note: No official source we could read describes mobile money; the tip now gives the UK's cash advice.

entries.old: The main tourist areas — Douala, Yaoundé and Kribi — see mostly trouble-free visits …
entries.new: UK, Canada and Australia advice
entries.note: Unsourced reassurance about Douala, Yaoundé and Kribi removed.

entries.old: True
entries.new: False
entries.note: No official source we could read states that tap water is safe to drink across Canada (Health Canada describes shared provincial/municipal responsibility, not a nationwide statement).
Seasonal recommendation withdrawn; text now states FCDO weather periods.

entries.old: Firearms must be declared in writing; most handguns are prohibited
entries.new: Declare all firearms; visitors cannot import prohibited firearms, devices or weapons
entries.note: Rewritten to CBSA; "most handguns are prohibited" is not stated there.

entries.old: undeclared items carry steep on-the-spot fines
entries.new: banned food is confiscated and you could be fined (UK FCDO)
entries.note: Rewritten to the FCDO wording.

entries.old: Export of rough diamonds, gold and other minerals without a license is strictly prohibited.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says it is only legal to buy diamonds or precious stones through government-authorised agents.
entries.note: Rewritten to what UK FCDO advice states; the mineral-export licence claim is not in an official source.

entries.old: Photography of government buildings, airports and anything military is forbidden without a permit.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says you often need permission to take photos in public places, and that photographing government property, uniformed officers or military installations and personnel can get you detained, fined and your camera confiscated.
entries.note: Rewritten to what UK FCDO advice states; the mineral-export licence claim is not in an official source.

entries.old: Check your government's travel advice before even planning a trip — most currently advise against all travel to the Central African Republic, and insurance policies are often void in do-not-travel zones.
entries.new: The UK FCDO advises against all travel to the Central African Republic except Bangui, and against all but essential travel to Bangui; Australia advises against all travel. The FCDO warns that travel insurance could be invalidated if you travel against its advice.
entries.note: Rewritten to official travel advice.

entries.old: The one destination that draws travelers — Dzanga-Sangha's lowland gorillas and forest elephants — is only realistically visited on a fully organized trip via the park's official operators, usually entering through Bangui.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: Claims about how Dzanga-Sangha is visited are not stated by an official source.

entries.old: Bring all the money you will need in cash (CFA francs or euros to exchange). Cards and ATMs cannot be relied on anywhere in the country.
entries.new: Bring the money you will need in cash. The UK FCDO says there are very few ATMs and most places, including hotels, do not accept international cards; Canada says currency can be exchanged only in Bangui and Berbérati.
entries.note: Rewritten to official travel advice.

entries.old: No — most governments advise against all travel. Armed groups remain active across much of the country and the security situation can deteriorate quickly, including in Bangui. The few travelers who visit Dzanga-Sangha do so on fully organized trips with security arrangements.
entries.new: No. The UK FCDO advises against all travel outside Bangui and all but essential travel to Bangui, and Australia advises against all travel. Both say armed groups remain active and that violence can break out without warning, including in Bangui.
entries.note: Dzanga-Sangha claim removed; rewritten to official travel advice.

entries.old: General: 17
entries.new: Police: 2020; Fire and ambulance: 1212
entries.note: 17 is not listed by any official source; the UK FCDO gives 2020 for police and 1212 for fire and ambulance, and Canada also lists 2020 for police.

entries.old: November to February … the season for Zakouma National Park and expeditions to the Ennedi massif
entries.new: Rainy-season facts from the Government of Canada; no official seasonal guidance
entries.note: The UK FCDO advises against all travel to the Ennedi provinces; the seasonal claims had no official source.

entries.old: Photography requires care: photographing military sites, government buildings or airports without a permit is illegal. | Export of animal products and cultural artefacts without authorization is prohibited.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says it is illegal to photograph military sites, government buildings or airports without a permit, and the Government of Canada says a government permit is required for all photography.
entries.note: The note on exporting animal products and cultural artefacts had no official source.

entries.old: Zakouma National Park — one of Africa's great conservation revivals — is Chad's standout draw; visits run November to April and are best booked through the park's official operators well in advance.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: The park season and booking claims had no official source.

entries.new: ambulance 131, fire 132, police 133

entries.note: No official source we could read states that tap water here is safe to drink.

entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official page we could read supports this.

entries.old: Chile's agricultural border controls are among the strictest anywhere: no fresh fruit, vegetables, seeds, honey, meat, dairy or untreated wood, including items bought in the airport of departure.
entries.new: Chilean law requires every traveller to declare under oath, on the SAG form, any plants, animals, products of plant or animal origin (including handicrafts), agricultural chemicals or animal feed they bring in. Inspectors of the Agricultural and Livestock Service (SAG) check them whatever the quantity, destroy what does not meet the rules, and failing to declare risk products leads to sanctions and fines.

entries.old: Foreign visitors are exempt from Chile's 19% VAT on hotel stays when paying in US dollars with a foreign card or cash. Present your passport and electronic TUM at check-in. Many hotels will not apply it unless you ask.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official page we could read supports this.

entries.old: Chile is over 4,000 km long. Santiago to Punta Arenas is a four-hour flight, and the Atacama and Patagonia are effectively different trips. Plan domestic flights rather than buses for the long legs.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official page we could read supports this.

entries.old: Mobile payment via Alipay and WeChat Pay dominates — both now let foreign visitors link international Visa/Mastercard cards, which is the single most useful thing to set up before arrival. Foreign cards are rarely accepted directly at the point of sale, and cash acceptance is patchy outside banks and larger shops.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office says cashless payments through apps such as WeChat or Alipay are almost universal, and that outside major cities credit cards are not always accepted and ATMs are limited. Canada's travel advice says these platforms let foreign travellers link an international credit card, that international cards are accepted in many hotels and larger establishments but not universally, and that using foreign currency for everyday transactions is illegal.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the FCDO and Canada state.

entries.old: April–May and September–October offer the most comfortable weather across most of the country; summer is hot and rainy, and northern winters are harsh.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit China. The UK Foreign Office says the typhoon season normally runs from May to November, affecting southern and eastern coastal regions, and that flooding and storms are common in those months.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the comfort-season claims had no official source.

entries.old: ["Fingerprints are collected from most foreign nationals aged 14–70 on arrival.", "Duty-free allowance for visitors: 400 cigarettes and 1.5 liters of alcohol (over 12% vol).", "Printed or digital material deemed harmful to China's political interests can be confiscated; drones and satellite communication equipment may require registration."]
entries.new: ["Canada's travel advice says Chinese immigration officials take and keep the fingerprints of travellers aged 14 to 70 on entry, with some exceptions.", "Canada's travel advice says there are absolute prohibitions on importing arms, drugs, and plant or animal products that could carry disease or pests, and restrictions on printed material, film, photos and recordings considered detrimental to China's interests.", "The UK Foreign Office says the import, possession and use of drones are strictly regulated; contact the Civil Aviation Administration of China before travel."]
entries.note: Removed the unsourced 400-cigarette / 1.5-litre allowance and satellite-equipment claim; attributed the rest to Canada and the FCDO.

entries.old: Cards are widely accepted in city restaurants, hotels and malls, but cash rules in markets, small towns, taxis and rural areas. Carry small COP notes; ATMs are plentiful in cities. Use ones inside banks or malls.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office says credit and debit cards are widely accepted in hotels, shops and restaurants, and that US dollars and euros can be exchanged at banks and authorised money exchanges — not on the street.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the cited official source says.
Months that fall in the rainy season named by the cited source were removed.

entries.old: December to March is the main dry season across most of the country; July and August bring a second drier window. Being equatorial, Colombia varies more by altitude than by season.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Colombia's rainy seasons usually run from March to June and from September to November, and that the Atlantic and Caribbean hurricane season runs from early June to the end of November.
entries.note: Rewritten to the climate statement the cited source makes.

entries.old: Exporting pre-Columbian artefacts, coca leaf products and wildlife is illegal and heavily penalized.
entries.new: (removed or rewritten)
entries.note: Not stated by an official source we could read; removed or replaced with what the source says.

entries.old: Personal duty-free allowance is generally up to USD 1,500 of goods in addition to personal effects.
entries.new: (removed or rewritten)
entries.note: Not stated by an official source we could read; removed or replaced with what the source says.

entries.old: Do not hail taxis on the street at night. Use app-based services (Uber, DiDi, Cabify) or hotel-arranged cars. Keep phones out of sight on the street and be wary of overly friendly strangers offering food or drinks.
entries.new: Do not hail taxis on the street. The UK Foreign Office reports express kidnappings, assaults and robberies in unlicensed taxis and advises using licensed telephone or internet-based taxi services, or booking through your hotel; at Bogotá's El Dorado airport only authorised taxis may pick up passengers.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Bogotá sits at 2,640 m. Take it easy on arrival, hydrate, and go light on alcohol for the first day or two. Tap water is safe in Bogotá and Medellín; stick to bottled water on the coast and in rural areas.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says Bogotá lies about 2,600 m above sea level and that high-altitude illness is possible in parts of the country. Take it easy on arrival. The UK Foreign Office says tap water is safe to drink only in Bogotá; elsewhere drink bottled water and avoid ice.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed.

entries.old: Carry your yellow fever certificate if you plan to visit Tayrona, the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta or the Amazon — vaccination is checked for park entry and must be done at least 10 days before travel.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: Withdrawn: no official source we could read supports it.

entries.old: May to October is the cooler, drier season — the best window…; the November–April rains…
entries.new: Rainy season December–April (Government of Canada); cyclones January–May (UK FCDO).
entries.note: Rainy-season months corrected to the official sources; "best window" claims removed.

entries.old: safe to drink
entries.new: not for drinking
entries.note: Australia's Smartraveller advises boiled or bottled water.

entries.old: Cards are accepted almost everywhere tourists go, and US dollars are accepted nearly universally (change comes in colones, often at a poor rate). Keep some colones in cash for sodas (small local restaurants), rural areas, buses and tips.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says credit cards are widely accepted and most international hotels and tourist facilities take credit and debit cards, but advises carrying cash for rural areas. Canada's travel advice adds that US dollars are easier to exchange than Canadian dollars and that cash withdrawals need a 4-digit PIN.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official travel advice says, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: December to April is the dry season ("verano") on the Pacific side — the most reliable weather for beaches and wildlife; the green season (May–November) is cheaper and lush, with mostly-sunny mornings and afternoon downpours.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says heavy rains, particularly from mid-May to the end of November, can cause severe flooding and landslides, and that the hurricane season runs from mid-May (Pacific) or early June (Caribbean) to the end of November.
entries.note: Replaced with the climate statement the cited source supports.

entries.old: Duty-free allowance: 500 g of tobacco and 5 liters of alcoholic beverages per adult. | Strict biosecurity rules apply to fresh fruit, plants, seeds and animal products. Declare them or leave them at home. | The USD 29 air departure charge (USD 27 tax plus USD 2 baggage scanning) is included in the ticket by most airlines — if yours does not include it, pay it at the airport before check-in.
entries.new: When leaving by air you may need to pay a departure tax of USD 29; the UK government says most airlines include it in the ticket price, and if you have to pay it you can use cash or card.
entries.note: Only what an official source states is kept, attributed; unsupported claims removed.

entries.old: Renting a car? Mandatory local liability insurance is added on top of quoted prices (budget for it), never leave anything in a parked car, and check whether your route needs 4x4 — some beach-town roads involve unbridged river crossings that rental contracts often exclude.
entries.new: Renting a car? Never leave anything in a parked car — Australia's Smartraveller says criminals target stationary cars and rental vehicles for robberies — and check whether your route needs 4x4.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Rip currents are the leading cause of tourist deaths in Costa Rica. Many popular beaches have no lifeguards. If caught, swim parallel to the shore until free of the current, then in.
entries.new: The UK government says rip currents are very common on Costa Rica's beaches, there are often no lifeguards, and drownings are the second most common cause of accidental death. Get reliable local advice before swimming.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.old: Tap water is safe to drink in most of Costa Rica, including San José and the main tourist towns; in remote coastal or rural spots, ask locally or use bottled water.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller advises drinking boiled or bottled water in Costa Rica.
entries.note: Rewritten to what official sources state, attributed.

entries.note: The UK, Canadian and Australian advice list three police numbers: 110, 111 and 170.

entries.old: ["French", "Baoulé", "Dioula"]
entries.new: ["French"]
entries.note: French is the only official language under Article 48 of the Constitution; Baoulé and Dioula are not official languages.

entries.old: Cards are accepted at hotels, supermarkets and better restaurants in Abidjan, but cash and mobile money (Wave, Orange Money, MTN) dominate everywhere else. Carry CFA francs outside the big cities.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says credit cards are accepted at major hotels and some restaurants and shops, ATMs are available in Abidjan and most major cities, and you should carry cash outside major cities. Australia's Smartraveller adds that Abidjan's ATMs may not be reliable and ATMs are rare outside the city.
entries.note: Rewritten to Canada's and Australia's advice; card acceptance lowered from 'widely in cities' to 'limited', and the mobile-money claims had no source.

entries.old: December to March is the driest stretch on the coast — good for Abidjan, Grand-Bassam and Assinie; May to July brings the heaviest rain in the south.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice gives the rainy seasons as May to July and October to November on the southern coast, mid-March to mid-May and mid-July to mid-October in the centre, and July to November in the north. No official source names a best season; the months shown fall outside the coastal rains.
entries.note: Replaced with the rainy seasons given by Canada.

entries.old: Yellow fever certificates are checked systematically at Abidjan airport, before immigration. Keep the yellow card with your passport.
entries.new: You must have a yellow fever vaccination certificate to enter Côte d'Ivoire, and Australia's Smartraveller says you may be asked to show it when you leave, including by some airlines. Keep it with your passport.
entries.note: The claim that certificates are checked systematically before immigration had no source.

entries.old: Avoid the northern border zones with Mali and Burkina Faso, including the northern fringe of Comoé National Park — jihadist groups have carried out attacks there.
entries.new: The UK, Canadian and Australian governments warn of a terrorist threat in the northern border areas with Mali and Burkina Faso, including Comoé National Park. Australia advises against all travel to the Folon, Bagoué, Poro, Bounkani and Tchologo regions and the north of Zanzan and Savanes.
entries.note: Attributed to the three governments and aligned with the areas they name.

entries.old: Mobile money is everywhere — Wave and Orange Money QR codes work for taxis, maquis restaurants and market stalls where cards never will.
entries.new: (removed)
entries.note: No official source supports this tip.

entries.old: Pre-enroll only through the official SNEDAI service — unofficial eVisa sites charge heavy mark-ups and cannot speed up the airport counter.
entries.new: Apply for the e-visa only through the official service that Canada's travel advice links to, snedai.com.
entries.note: The mark-up claim about unofficial sites had no source.

entries.old: Abidjan, the coast and the central regions are generally fine for travelers who take normal big-city precautions. The far north along the Mali and Burkina Faso borders carries a real terrorism risk and is best avoided. Check current advisories before overland travel.
entries.new: Canada, the UK and Australia all warn of a terrorist threat throughout the country, highest in the northern regions bordering Mali and Burkina Faso, where Australia advises against all travel to the Folon, Bagoué, Poro, Bounkani and Tchologo regions and the north of Zanzan and Savanes. Check current advisories before travelling.
entries.note: 'Generally fine' for Abidjan and the centre was not what the advisories say: they warn of a nationwide terrorist threat.

entries.new: false

entries.old: {"cardsAccepted": "widely", "text": "Croatia adopted the euro in January 2023. Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere; keep some cash for small konobas, markets and island kiosks."}

entries.old: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
entries.new: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU's Your Europe portal lists duty-free allowances of 1 litre of spirits (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine), 4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer and other goods worth up to €300 (€430 by air or sea). For tobacco, Croatia applies the lower limit of 40 cigarettes to travellers arriving by land or sea; the higher limit is 200 cigarettes.
entries.note: Correction: Croatia applies the EU's lower tobacco allowance (40 cigarettes) to travellers arriving by land or sea; 200 applies only by air.

entries.old: No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
entries.new: Between EU countries, alcohol and tobacco bought for your own use and not for resale carry no further duty, but customs can check the quantities against guideline levels, according to Your Europe.
entries.note: 'No limits' overstated it: customs can check quantities against guideline levels.

entries.new: (removed)

entries.old: Entering Cyprus through airports or ports in the Turkish-occupied north (e.g. Ercan) is treated as illegal entry by the Republic of Cyprus. Arrive via the south (Larnaca or Paphos). You can then cross to the north and back at recognized checkpoints with your passport.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says that if you enter through the north (for example Ercan Airport), the Republic of Cyprus considers you to have entered illegally: you could be fined or prevented from crossing back into the north. Entering through the south, you can use any crossing point to move between north and south.
entries.note: Rewritten to UK FCDO advice.

entries.old: Cyprus drives on the left, a legacy of British rule. Take extra care at roundabouts and when picking up a rental car, and note that rural roads can be narrow and winding.
entries.new: Traffic drives on the left in Cyprus, according to Canada's travel advice and the US CDC. Canada adds that vehicle insurance bought in the Republic of Cyprus is not valid in the north, including for rental cars.
entries.note: Historical and road-condition claims removed; rewritten to official sources.

entries.old: Days spent in Cyprus do not count against your Schengen 90/180 allowance — Cyprus is EU but not Schengen — making it a popular stop for travelers resetting their Schengen days.
entries.new: The UK FCDO says Cyprus is not part of the Schengen area, so visits to Cyprus do not count towards your 90-day visa-free limit in Schengen, and Schengen days do not count towards your limit in Cyprus.
entries.note: Unsupported claim about travellers resetting Schengen days removed.

entries.old: July and August regularly exceed 35–40°C inland. Plan sightseeing at ancient sites like Kourion and Paphos for early morning, and carry water.
entries.new: Australia's Smartraveller says summer heatwaves are becoming more frequent: drink plenty of water, wear light clothing, stay in air conditioning or shade, and follow local authorities' advice.
entries.note: Temperature figures are not stated by an official source; rewritten.

entries.old: Yes, by crossing at recognized checkpoints (such as Ledra Street in Nicosia) with your passport after entering through the south. Arriving directly in the north via Ercan airport or northern ports is considered illegal entry by the Republic of Cyprus and can cause problems, including refusal of entry in the south.
entries.new: Yes, by crossing at a designated crossing point after entering through the south — Canada says crossing the UN buffer zone anywhere else is illegal. The UK FCDO says entering through the north, for example via Ercan Airport, is treated by the Republic of Cyprus as illegal entry and can lead to a fine or to being prevented from crossing back into the north.
entries.note: Rewritten to official travel advice.

entries.old: The left, like the UK, Ireland and Malta. Rental cars are right-hand drive with distinctive red plates, and speed limits are posted in kilometers per hour.
entries.new: The left. Canada's travel advice and the US CDC both say traffic drives on the left in Cyprus. Canada adds that you must be at least 18 to drive and can use a Canadian licence for up to 6 months.
entries.note: Rental plate and comparison claims removed; rewritten to official sources.

entries.old: Cards and contactless accepted almost everywhere
entries.new: No official description of card acceptance
entries.note: The card-acceptance claim had no official source and was withdrawn.

entries.new: (removed)

entries.old: Photography of airports, bridges, borders and government or military sites is prohibited and enforced.
entries.new: Canada's travel advice says photographing government buildings, airports or military installations is forbidden, under penalty of arrest or detention.

entries.old: Denmark is close to cashless. Cards and mobile payments (MobilePay) work everywhere, and some shops no longer accept cash at all. There is little need to exchange money.
entries.new: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Denmark. Canada's travel advice says some stores add a surcharge when you pay with a foreign credit card.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the 'close to cashless' and MobilePay claims had no official source.

entries.old: May to August offers long, bright days for Copenhagen, the coast and cycling; winters are dark and wet, though December has cosy Christmas markets and Tivoli lights.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Denmark. The CIA World Factbook describes a temperate, humid and overcast climate with mild, windy winters and cool summers.
entries.note: Withdrawn: the seasonal claims had no official source.

Under-17s get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.", "Between EU countries there is no fixed limit on goods for your own use, but Denmark may set guideline quantities for alcohol and tobacco, which cannot be lower than 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits.", "The UK Foreign Office says you cannot take meat, milk or products containing them into the EU, with some exceptions such as powdered baby milk and medically required foods.", "The UK Foreign Office says it is illegal to import whale products from Greenland or the Faroe Islands into the UK or EU."]

entries.old: Cards are accepted at the bigger hotels and restaurants in Djibouti City, but everywhere else runs on cash. US dollars are widely accepted alongside the Djiboutian franc, and ATMs are essentially confined to the capital.
entries.new: The UK Foreign Office says credit and debit cards are not widely accepted, and where they are you often need a Visa card. ATMs are normally available in Djibouti City but may not accept Mastercard, so carry enough cash.
entries.note: Rewritten to what the cited official source says.

entries.old: November to March brings the coolest weather, and the whale shark season in the Gulf of Tadjoura (roughly November to February) plus comfortable conditions for Lake Assal and the Danakil landscapes; summer heat is extreme.
entries.new: No official source we could read gives seasonal travel guidance for Djibouti.

entries.old: Khat is legal and widely consumed in Djibouti, but carrying it out of the country can be a serious offense at your next destination.

entries.new: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to the Djibouti–Eritrea border, and Canada advises against non-essential travel within 10 km of it. There are unmarked landmines near the border.
